title: One value, four printf conversions
request: Teach me how printf shows the same int with %d, %u, %f and %c, as all six media.

diagnostics.clang:
ub.c:5:20: warning: format specifies type 'double' but the argument has type 'int' [-Wformat]
    5 |     printf("%f\n", a);
      |             ~~     ^
      |             %d
1 warning generated.
diagnostics.gcc-16:
ub.c: In function 'main':
ub.c:5:14: warning: format '%f' expects argument of type 'double', but argument 2 has type 'int' [-Wformat=]
    5 |     printf("%f\n", a);

      |              |     |

claims.text: The program stores 66 in the int a.
claims.justification: views.c line 5 is int a = 66;.

claims.text: a is an int, 4 bytes on this machine. 66 fits in its low byte: 01000010, which is 0x42 in hex.
claims.justification: sizeof(int) is 4 on this platform (captured platform fact; LP64). 66 < 256, so the value lies entirely in the least significant byte; the program prints bits 7..0 of a with a shift loop (01000010) and (unsigned)a with %#x (0x42).

sources.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), working draft N2176
sources.quote: For signed integer types, the bits of the object representation shall be divided into three groups: value bits, padding bits, and the sign bit.

claims.text: %d formats an int as a signed decimal number, so for a = 66 it gives 66.
claims.justification: 7.21.6.1p8, conversion d: the int argument is converted to signed decimal. a is 66; the run printed 66 on line 3.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), working draft N2176
sources.quote: The int argument is converted to signed decimal in the style [−]dddd.

claims.text: (unsigned)a converts 66 to unsigned int. 66 is representable there, so the value stays 66 and %u gives 66.
claims.justification: 6.3.1.3p1: a value representable in the new integer type is unchanged; 66 is representable in unsigned int. %u converts an unsigned int to unsigned decimal (7.21.6.1p8). The run printed 66 on line 4.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), working draft N2176
sources.quote: When a value with integer type is converted to another integer type other than _Bool, if the value can be represented by the new type, it is unchanged.

claims.text: (double)a converts the value 66 to the double 66.0. On this machine, where double is IEC 60559 binary64, that double's bits are 0x4050800000000000, not the bits of a.
claims.justification: 6.3.1.4p2: an integer value exactly representable in the floating type is unchanged, so the result is 66.0. On this platform double has the binary64 parameters that C17 §5.2.4.2.2 EXAMPLE 2 gives for an IEC 60559 double: programs/double_format.c prints FLT_RADIX 2, DBL_MANT_DIG 53, DBL_MIN_EXP -1021 and DBL_MAX_EXP 1024 (facts f.radix, f.mantdig, f.minexp, f.maxexp), and sizeof(double) is 8 (f.dsize). The format is measured, not taken from Annex F, which binds only implementations that define __STDC_IEC_559__. Its encoding of 66 = 1.03125 x 2^6 is sign 0, biased exponent 1023 + 6 = 1029 = 0x405 and fraction 0.03125 = 2^-5, giving 0x4050800000000000. Lines 15-18 copy the double's bytes into an unsigned long long with memcpy and print them; the run printed 0x4050800000000000, while a's own value is 0x42.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), working draft N2176
sources.quote: When a value of integer type is converted to a real floating type, if the value being converted can be represented exactly in the new type, it is unchanged.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), working draft N2176
sources.quote: The following describes floating-point representations that also meet the requirements for single-precision and double-precision numbers in IEC 60559, and the appropriate values in a <float.h> header for types float and double:

claims.text: %f prints a finite double with six digits after the decimal point when no precision is given, so it prints 66.000000.
claims.justification: 7.21.6.1p8, conversion f: style [−]ddd.ddd with precision digits after the point; a missing precision is taken as 6. The argument is the double 66.0; the run printed 66.000000 on line 5.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), working draft N2176
sources.quote: A double argument representing a floating-point number is converted to decimal notation in the style [−]ddd.ddd, where the number of digits after the decimal-point character is equal to the precision specification. If the precision is missing, it is taken as 6

claims.text: %c converts the int 66 to unsigned char and writes that character. In ASCII, code 66 is B.
claims.justification: 7.21.6.1p8, conversion c without l: the int argument is converted to an unsigned char and the resulting character is written. The execution character set here is ASCII (macOS), where 66 is 'B'. The run printed B on line 6.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), working draft N2176
sources.quote: If no l length modifier is present, the int argument is converted to an unsigned char, and the resulting character is written.

claims.text: In views.c, %f receives the double that (double)a made, not a itself, so printf does not reinterpret the bits of a for %f.
claims.justification: Scoped to views.c line 13, printf("%f\n", (double)a): the argument expression is (double)a, of type double, so the value passed through the ellipsis is the double 66.0 (6.5.2.2p7: trailing arguments get the default argument promotions; a double stays a double), and %f converts that double argument (7.21.6.1p8). The int's bits are never what %f reads in views.c. The sentence says nothing about ub.c, which passes a itself and is undefined (c.ub).

sources.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), working draft N2176
sources.quote: The ellipsis notation in a function prototype declarator causes argument type conversion to stop after the last declared parameter. The default argument promotions are performed on trailing arguments.

claims.text: Without the cast, printf("%f\n", a) passes an int where %f needs a double, and the behaviour is undefined.
claims.justification: 7.21.6.1p9: if any argument is not the correct type for its conversion specification, the behavior is undefined. %f requires a double; a is an int. The recorded diagnostics for ub.c flag line 5 (gcc-16: format '%f' expects argument of type 'double', but argument 2 has type 'int').

sources.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), working draft N2176
sources.quote: If any argument is not the correct type for the corresponding conversion specification, the behavior is undefined.

claims.text: So ub.c is compiled for its warning and never run.
claims.justification: lesson.json marks ub.c ub: true and run: false; ptk compiles it, records the warning, and never runs it, so no output of it is shown.

claims.text: With %d, %u, %f and %c, the value stays 66; %c writes it as the character with code 66. (unsigned)a keeps a's bits too, since 66 has the same representation in int and unsigned int. (double)a changes the type and the bits.
claims.justification: Line 11 passes a to %d (66). Line 12 passes (unsigned)a: 66 is representable in unsigned int, so the value is unchanged (6.3.1.3p1), and a nonnegative value has the same representation in a signed type and its unsigned type (6.2.5p9), so (unsigned)a has a's bits. Line 13 passes (double)a, the double 66.0: the value is unchanged (6.3.1.4p2), but the type is double and its bits on this machine are 0x4050800000000000 (run line 7), not a's. Line 14 passes a to %c, which converts it to unsigned char 66 (7.21.6.1p8) and writes B. The run printed 66, 66, 66.000000 and B on lines 3-6.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), working draft N2176
sources.quote: The range of nonnegative values of a signed integer type is a subrange of the corresponding unsigned integer type, and the representation of the same value in each type is the same.

claims.text: For a = 200, %d and %u both print 200, because 200 is not negative and fits in both int and unsigned int.
claims.justification: C17 6.3.1.3p1: converting a value that the new type can represent leaves it unchanged; 200 is representable in unsigned int, so (unsigned)a is 200 and %u prints 200; %d prints the int 200. Captured run of views_200.c lines 3-4.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), working draft N2176
sources.quote: if the value can be represented by the new type, it is unchanged.

claims.text: %c converts 200 to unsigned char, which on this machine holds 0 to 255, so it keeps 200. That byte is outside ASCII, which stops at 127, so what a terminal draws for it depends on its encoding.
claims.justification: C17 7.21.6.1p8: for %c the int argument is converted to unsigned char and that character is written. 200 is representable in unsigned char (UCHAR_MAX is 255), so the byte written is 200; the program records it by formatting %c into a buffer with snprintf and printing the byte as a number. ASCII defines codes 0 to 127 only.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), working draft N2176
sources.quote: the int argument is converted to an unsigned char, and the resulting character is written.

claims.text: On this machine, where unsigned int is 32 bits, (unsigned)-1 adds 2^32 once, so %u prints 4294967295 while %d prints -1.
claims.justification: C17 6.3.1.3p2: a negative value converted to an unsigned type is brought into range by adding one more than the maximum value of the new type. unsigned int is 32 bits here (sizeof(int) is 4), so -1 + 4294967296 = 4294967295. %d prints the int -1. Captured run of views_m1.c lines 3-4.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), working draft N2176
sources.quote: the value is converted by repeatedly adding or subtracting one more than the maximum value that can be represented in the new type until the value is in the range of the new type.

claims.text: On this machine, where unsigned char holds 0 to 255, %c converts -1 by adding 256, which gives the byte 255, outside ASCII.
claims.justification: C17 7.21.6.1p8 converts the %c argument to unsigned char; by 6.3.1.3p2, -1 + (UCHAR_MAX + 1) = -1 + 256 = 255. ASCII stops at 127. The program prints the byte %c produced: 255.

claims.text: On this machine, with 8-bit bytes, 321 does not fit in one byte. Its low byte is 01000001, which is 0x41, and %d and %u still print 321.
claims.justification: 321 = 256 + 65, so bits 7..0 of a are 01000001 (0x41); the int value 321 is unchanged, so %d prints 321 and (unsigned)a is 321 for %u. Captured run of views_321.c lines 1-4.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), working draft N2176
sources.quote: For signed integer types, the bits of the object representation shall be divided into three groups: value bits, padding bits, and the sign bit.

claims.text: On this machine, where unsigned char holds 0 to 255, %c converts 321 by subtracting 256, which leaves 65, and code 65 is A in ASCII.
claims.justification: C17 7.21.6.1p8 converts the %c argument to unsigned char; by 6.3.1.3p2, 321 - 256 = 65. ASCII code 65 is the letter A. The program prints the byte %c produced: 65.

claims.text: For each of these four values, (double)a converts the value exactly, and %f prints it with six digits after the point.
claims.justification: C17 6.3.1.4p2: an integer converted to a real floating type that can represent it exactly is unchanged in value; every int here (66, 200, -1, 321) is exact in double. 7.21.6.1p8 %f: six digits after the decimal point when the precision is missing. Captured runs: 66.000000, 200.000000, -1.000000, 321.000000.
